Morning update, Sat 28 Nov. Tehran spent Friday promising to break the US blockade, and CENTCOM answered by showing a ship it had stopped. The Palau-flagged Pacific Archer left Bandar Abbas and was struck at the stern in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday, disclosed last night. I think the blockade is holding, and the harder words from Tehran are covering for that rather than announcing a breakout.

Hormuz. CENTCOM says a US aircraft used precision munitions to disable the Pacific Archer's propulsion after "multiple warnings", and the civilian crew was unharmed. Its running count is six ships disabled and 158 turned back since the blockade was reinstated. There's no UKMTO report or independent position yet. Separately, the IRGC Navy claims on state TV that a tanker struck a mine and exploded north of Ghanam Island, with a second turning back. No ship named, no time given, and it may be Thursday's two-tanker claim coming round again.

Tehran. Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to the Supreme Leader: "Neither will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened, nor will we allow the blockade to remain in place." Navy commander Shahram Irani says breaking the blockade "is underway", that Iran's ports are operating and that ships are getting escorts. He also claims Iran struck the USS Abraham Lincoln early in the war, which nobody has confirmed. What's missing is a single named ship that's got out. The IRGC itself says tankers using "unauthorised routes" have dropped sharply in recent days, which reads to me like the pressure biting on both sides of the strait.

Doha and Islamabad. Araghchi says the Qatari and Pakistani mediators are still passing proposals and Tehran is reviewing them, but Hormuz opens only once Iran's demands are met. Nothing new from Oman overnight.

Israel. The security cabinet is due to meet on Sunday, reportedly on Trump's Gaza plan (Channel 12): facilities for an international stabilisation force deploying from January and a pilot humanitarian zone in Rafah. Iran isn't on the reported agenda, and I've still seen no outcome from the meeting flagged for Thursday. Eisenkot has about eight days left on his mandate and says he'll form a government without asking for more time.

Saudi Arabia. The coalition reported two more Houthi drones intercepted heading for the Riyadh region on Friday, a day after the projectile strike on the Jazan refinery that killed a worker.

Markets. Brent settled at $95.44 on Friday, down 1.2%, but still up about 3% on the week. OPEC+ meets on Sunday and is expected to hold output.

Today I'm watching for one thing: a named ship that has actually run the blockade, or CENTCOM announcing a seventh one disabled.

50bps hike in December by RBI MPC, if it happens, will be a mistake. 6% CPI YoY on a base of zero CPI YoY is what we have. Broad money growth has happened in part due to FCNR deposits, partially sterilised via CRR etc (now being reversed), core-core inflation remains about headline target. And Chinese industrial over-capacity weighs as can be seen in their overall and our bilateral trade numbers despite our various efforts.

Moreover, crude has somewhat corrected and the rupee has somewhat appreciated. There is no reason to do a double hike - the so called credibility crowd will never be convinced because they do not use quantifiable models rather Calvinist 'economics' where pain is always good. Indian potential/trend growth, sustainable growth that can happen without broad demand side inflation overheating, seems higher than consensus. Food inflation/bad monsoon effects should also roll over next year.

We should have more explicit usage of modified Taylor or various real rates models. We must push for an Indian TIPS market so we have a better handle of Indian expected inflation over and above deeply imperfect surveys (not that TIPS are fully perfect.) But to simultaneously hear of low wage growth, productivity adjusted even more so, and incipient inflation is jarring except in a faith-based ideological narrow argument.

Last year we had two quarters (not months) of below 2% (lower band) average Indian inflation: we came close to the three-quarter limit. We have not remotely shot equally on the other side. We must not be so dismissive of the growth impact. Macro stability does not mean a low-growth trap, with some future high-growth utopia always. We have to be reasonably inflation-targeting within the given framework. Credibility comes from persistence not panic.

The case for no December hike.

Gold is down five and a half percent from its November thirteenth peak. WTI is off six percent. Brent five. The ten-year has fallen twenty-one basis points from five point one five to four point nine four. Three disinflation inputs, one direction, over two weeks. The market is doing the Fed's work before the Fed does.

Energy pass-through is complete. Oil's monthly decline of nineteen to twenty-one percent has already hit pump prices and freight costs. Where is the next inflation impulse supposed to come from? Services and shelter lag — they follow, they don't lead.

Housing is in a recession. Existing sales at three point seven five million annualized, slowest since twenty ten. Builder confidence at twenty-five, lowest since twenty twelve. Forty-six percent of builders cutting prices. Inventory at five point one months. Ninety-five percent of borrowers sit below today's rates. Another hike doesn't cool a frozen market — it forces sellers into a market with no buyers. That's destabilizing, not disinflationary.

Commercial real estate is the hidden systemic risk. Regional banks are carrying office and retail loans at values that stopped being real years ago. Force the mark-to-market and capital ratios crack. The Fed cannot hike into banking stress — March twenty twenty-three proved that.

Sovereign and AI debt levels are at historic highs. Every quarter point raises the government's interest expense, which is now one of the largest line items in the federal budget, and feeds straight back into inflation. The tool meant to cool prices reheats them through the fiscal channel.

Warsh is a Greenspan disciple. Greenspan trusted financial conditions to do the tightening. They have. Holding in December isn't inaction — it's reading the tape.

On Waller: calling for a half-point hike or a faster twenty twenty-seven pace ignores every input above. He's not being hawkish. He's being blind. Pre-committing to a path before the data arrives isn't resolve — it's the credibility cost of being wrong in public.

Burden of proof is on the hawks now.

2126558220701614169.text:
Happy weekend fam, 

Crypto is finding its way back to good old Proof-of-Work. First privacy, now AI mining.

@naval's "Bitcoin is insurance against fiat. Zcash is insurance against Bitcoin" take helped kickstart one of the biggest narrative trades of this cycle.

$ZEC had an absurd run off the back of that, but it's now down 40% in 30d, and Grayscale's Zcash ETF saw $61M in outflows this month.

Meanwhile, many CT bros swap $ZEC for $PRL. In hindsight, it's pretty clear where CT's attention has been moving.

The market is getting tired after years of low-float launches, ridiculous FDVs, insider unlocks and retail effectively becoming exit liquidity for private investors…

Privacy brought back the cypherpunk side of crypto. AI mining is bringing back the idea that anyone with the right hardware can participate in token issuance.

Both also appeal to the idea of alternative money that offers something BTC doesn't.

Obviously, miner-driven distribution doesn't automatically mean fair distribution.

But I'd argue there's a pretty big difference between putting GPUs and electricity to work for new coins and getting in at a fraction of the price in a private round.

Some projects on my radar:

– @prlnet $PRL: replaces conventional PoW hashing with matrix multiplication, the same type of computation used in AI workloads.

– @bittensor $TAO: 128+ active subnets and a more established economy around incentivizing useful intelligence.

– @nockchain base:0x9b5e262cf9bb04869ab40b19af91d2dc85761722: running both ZK and AI PoW, with the ability to merge-mine alongside Pearl.

– @flop_labs solana:HwCG1Jr6RbAVsKX1qTaH6JtFYGeE6zaLd13W44YGpump: backed by @CryptoHayes, just launched its testnet with a design that puts demand for compute before execution.

– @ambient_xyz: experimenting with Proof of Logits to integrate AI inference into consensus.

– @gonka_ai: targeting decentralized AI computation with higher-end GPU requirements.

Different mechanisms, but all exploring how crypto incentives can coordinate computational resources.

The timing makes sense too.

Hyperscaler capex is on track to exceed $800B this year. 

Public Bitcoin miners have announced over $70B in AI/HPC contracts, with AI hosting estimated to generate 3x the profit per MW of BTC mining at current hash prices.

There's a very real economic reason for compute infrato move towards AI.

Everyone knows higher token price makes mining more profitable. More GPUs come online, hashrate goes up, network growth attracts attention on CT, new buyers come in.

But it works both ways.

Miners have electricity bills to pay, hardware to amortize, and no obligation to hold the coins they mine. Demand for mining a coin isn't the same as demand for the work being performed.

More hashrate also means more competition for the same emissions.

My thesis rn is that the market is pricing the return of PoW before it's pricing the utility of AI mining.

The privacy meta reminded us that crypto can still put a massive monetary premium on assets without conventional protocol revenues.

AI mining takes that same speculative appetite, adds permissionless participation, and attaches it to the biggest technological and capital expenditure cycle in the world.

That's a pretty compelling combination for an emerging meta, even in this miserable market.

The real opportunity lies in the projects that can eventually turn miners from recipients of token subsidies into providers of compute that somebody outside crypto is willing to pay for.

Twenty-eight days after the biggest hack in crypto history, Binance just reopened the doors. The money ran out faster than anyone expected.

On 26/11, Binance completed the restoration of withdrawals across nearly all networks — the end of a phased recovery from the 29/10 hack of $6.36 billion, the largest crypto theft ever. TRM Labs and the FBI attribute the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Withdrawals had been halted after the hack, then restored in phases from 1/11, starting with Bitcoin.

Binance says it used more than $6.34 billion of its own money to cover the losses. And when the doors first reopened on 1/11, the customers came for their money: in the first 9.5 hours, users pulled out a net $3.64 billion — $4.65 billion withdrawn against just $1.01 billion deposited.

But the story is not over. On the very same day, 26/11, the hacker moved another $35.52 million in ETH, according to Onchain Lens. About $1.9 billion remains unfrozen and in play — 461,980 ETH worth roughly $785.2 million, plus 18,350 BTC worth about $1.11 billion. Around $2.6–2.7 billion in stablecoins has been frozen. And on 23/11, the US Department of Justice moved to seize more than $1.1 billion in USDC.

Think about what just happened. The world's biggest exchange lost $6.36 billion, covered it from its own pocket, reopened withdrawals — and nearly $4 billion still walked out the door in less than ten hours. That is not a vote of no confidence. That is what a bank run looks like when the bank actually survives it.

The question now: did Binance just prove that even the biggest exchange can take a $6 billion hit and keep standing — or did the $3.64 billion that left in 9.5 hours prove that trust, once broken, never fully comes back?

Getting started requires connecting a wallet. There's no email registration or KYC. A one-time on-chain registration creates the trading account, while funds remain in your wallet. USDC is currently supported as collateral on Arbitrum and Solana.

The Markets section covers perpetual pairs like BTC, ETH, and SOL, alongside RWA markets. Traders can search assets or sort them by 24-hour price change, volume, and funding rate. Each market also provides mark price, index price, open interest, order book depth, and recent trades.

For execution, traders can open long or short positions using market or limit orders. Cross and isolated margin are supported, with leverage up to 100x depending on the market. TP and SL settings are also available. The Positions tab tracks unrealized PnL, entry price, liquidation price, and funding information.

The Portfolio section brings account value, margin, positions, and performance into one view.

There's also a Spot section supporting multiple networks, including Solana, Ethereum, BNB Chain, Base, Arc, and Robinhood Chain. It includes trending tokens, security metrics, one-click buying, and automated limit, trigger, TP, and SL orders that remain active offline. Spot trading currently has 0% platform fees.

I'm convinced that @metricxyz is becoming one of the biggest beneficiaries of the tokenized stock boom.

– Captured ~90% of ANTx volume and 97% of trades on Ethereum since launch

– Captured 75%+ of ANTB volume on BNB Chain since launch

– Recorded $123.6M in daily tokenized stock volume, second only to Aerodrome at $141.7M

Nearly $500M of the $1.2B volume Metric processed in its first 5 days after public launch came from tokenized stocks.

I don't think this is a coincidence. The way Metric approaches liquidity makes a lot more sense for assets whose prices are determined outside of crypto.

Take a tokenized NVIDIA stock. Nasdaq is where the vast majority of NVDA price discovery happens.

There's little economic reason for an onchain liquidity pool to repeatedly pay arbitrageurs to catch up with a price that already exists elsewhere.

And every time NVDA moves on earnings, macro news or whatever Jensen says, traditional LPs are exposed to stale quotes and potentially have to reposition their liquidity.

Metric approaches this differently with Active Pools. Prices come from external price providers, while liquidity sits in percentage-based bins relative to those prices.

When NVDA moves, the liquidity ranges move with it without LPs having to manually reposition their capital.

Less capital sitting at irrelevant prices, less value leaking to arbitrageurs and more usable liquidity near the market price.

Some comparisons I found particularly interesting:

– NVDAB on BNB Chain: Metric recorded 266x capital turnover vs 7.8x on PancakeSwap. Metric offered better fills in 70 out of 73 comparisons for $10k buys, with a median advantage of $17.

– META/USDG on RHC: a sampled $100k order cost $65 on Metric vs $935 on Uniswap v4.

– Against Binance: after accounting for Binance's taker fee, Metric offered better execution in 76 out of 87 completed comparisons for $100k tokenized stock sell orders.

An onchain exchange offering better execution than Binance on 6 figs stock trades is pretty wild.

Let @xStocksFi, @bstocksfinance, @Ondo and @RobinhoodCrypto fight it out over asset issuance and user acquisition.

Metric doesn't need to pick a side. It just needs to be the best place to trade their assets.

A trader swapping tokenized stocks through Binance Wallet or an aggregator doesn't necessarily know which DEX is filling the order.

Nor do they care, as long as they're getting a good fill.

Metric already understood this before its public launch. It processed $20B+ in its stealth phase, primarily through aggregator integrations, with only a few million dollars in liquidity.

Its distribution network now includes 0x, Kyber, Velora, Odos, OpenOcean, Enso and others.

Tokenized stock supply has grown from $700M early this year to $3.6B today, with 5M holders.

As more externally priced assets come onchain, I expect purpose-built liquidity venues to eat into the market share of traditional AMMs.

Metric is already showing what that could look like at scale.

2126550390506418446.text:
r/OpenAI spent 223 comments arguing that AI labs secretly solved P = NP.

Not one of them named the person who started the rumor.

I pulled 216 of those comments, plus the receipts behind them. What's in there is a clean anatomy of how a real breakthrough becomes a fake headline.

The last four weeks, in order:

Oct 26 — OpenAI says an internal model refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Subexponential. Not polynomial.

Nov 17 — Viola publishes an essay arguing P could equal NP. An opinion, not a proof — one of the two places this headline came from. (The other: crypto traders read "ETH is false" as Ethereum and sold.)

Nov 20 — a Claude-assisted Riemann proof is posted; Lean's kernel replays it. No human has signed off yet.

Nov 23 — Anthropic posts a VP≠VNP proof. OpenAI follows within hours. Both papers say: this does not settle P vs NP.

Nov 24 — Axios: 24+ insiders say unreleased models can't be shipped safely. The actual story of the week.

Nov 25 — Aaronson reports "many, many rumors" that a lab is sitting on Factoring in P. Then strikes the line through and calls it a game of Telephone.

That's the whole supply chain. No P=NP. No broken RSA. Clay still lists it as open.

Four gates separate a theorem from your bank account:

Proposition — ETH ≠ P=NP. VP≠VNP is the algebraic version, and its own abstract says so.

Construction — a proof of P=NP can be non-constructive. It proves an algorithm exists and never hands you one.

Scale — O(n^1000) is polynomial and also forever. One estimate puts the crossover near 10^10000 variables.
Deployment — RSA is one assumption; ECC and lattices are others. The hard part is signatures, firmware, protocol stacks: a decade of migration.
Meanwhile, in the thread: the top comment (158 upvotes) reads "solved but P is not NP and nothing changes." The correction sits at #3. The #2 comment (117) asks why 90s movies were better — that branch took 31% of the thread's comment karma. Technical caveats took 10%.

Why the meme works: it's a clip from Sneakers (1992), where a chip called "the codebreaker" opens the Fed, the grid, air traffic control. "No more secrets."

The project in the film is named SETEC ASTRONOMY — an anagram of TOO MANY SECRETS.

And the ending refuses to say who holds the chip. It only shows the effects.

That's the part worth sitting with. Every "it's solved" is unverifiable. Every "it isn't" is unfalsifiable. The one thing we can measure is attention — and attention went to the joke.

The scariest line this month isn't mathematical. It's from Axios: employees no longer believe these models can be released safely. Once that's in the air, every preprint starts to look like evidence of a cover-up. That belief is now self-sustaining whether or not a single rumor is true.

So before the next "AI broke cryptography" post, ask four things:

Which proposition? Does it construct an algorithm? Where's the crossover? Which deployed system actually breaks?

If it can't answer all four, it isn't news. It's a movie quote.

2126556172089999631.text:
AI Is Structural, and the Market Is Underestimating What Comes Next

After reading the 167-page Situational Awareness letter by Leopold Aschenbrenner and his team, published on November 24, 2026, I find myself largely on the same page with Leopold regarding the trajectory of artificial intelligence, the extraordinary scale of the economic transformation ahead, and the increasingly significant disconnect between what is happening inside the frontier AI laboratories and what financial markets are currently pricing into technology equities. We have consistently maintained that AI represents a structural technological revolution rather than another conventional investment cycle, and nothing in the recent market correction has fundamentally changed that assessment. If anything, the letter strengthens our conviction that investors are still underestimating the speed at which AI capabilities are advancing, the enormous amount of computing infrastructure that will be required, and the potential economic value that increasingly autonomous systems could generate over the coming years. We believe the market has become excessively preoccupied with near-term capital expenditure concerns and investment returns, while paying insufficient attention to the possibility that we are approaching a much more consequential phase of AI development.

Perhaps the most important argument in Leopold's letter concerns recursive self-improvement, or RSI, whereby increasingly capable AI systems begin accelerating the development of subsequent generations of AI models. Historically, improvements in AI capabilities were primarily driven by two factors: increasing computational resources and improving algorithmic efficiency, which together produced approximately tenfold annual growth in effective compute. What is changing now is that AI itself is becoming an increasingly important contributor to algorithmic progress. According to the figures presented in the letter, Anthropic's AI agents were already performing approximately 19 hours of work for every hour worked by a human researcher, while code shipped per engineer had increased more than 45-fold relative to its 2024 baseline. Leopold estimates that the pace of AI progress is already running approximately 1.5 to 2 times faster than its historical trajectory, with the possibility that 2027 could deliver the equivalent of three years of technological progress within a single calendar year. These are extraordinary projections, and their precise magnitude remains uncertain, but the underlying mechanism is becoming increasingly credible. Once AI systems become sufficiently capable of contributing meaningfully to their own research, software development, experimentation, and optimization, the traditional relationship between human research capacity and technological progress begins to change fundamentally.

This is precisely why we believe artificial superintelligence may be considerably closer than the market currently appreciates. The transition from conventional chatbots to reasoning models and autonomous agents has already occurred remarkably quickly, and the next stage could be even more consequential as individual agents evolve into highly persistent multi-agent systems capable of coordinating complex tasks over days or weeks with relatively limited human intervention. Leopold describes this as a transition from virtual interns to virtual departments, where hundreds of specialized agents operate under supervisory AI systems, collectively performing work that would historically require entire teams of human professionals. The implications extend far beyond software engineering, encompassing financial analysis, scientific research, legal services, corporate operations, engineering design, and eventually physical applications through robotics. We should be careful not to equate impressive performance in selected research or coding tasks with demonstrated general superintelligence, but the direction of progress is increasingly difficult to dismiss. In our view, the probability of achieving transformative, economically consequential AI capabilities within the next several years is meaningfully higher than what prevailing market valuations appear to imply.

The implications for capital expenditure are particularly important because we fundamentally disagree with the increasingly popular argument that the AI infrastructure investment cycle is approaching its peak. We do not believe aggregate AI-related capital expenditure will peak anytime soon, although individual companies may experience temporary pauses or fluctuations in spending. One of the most revealing charts in the letter appears on page 14, where Leopold compares his original forecasts for hyperscaler capital expenditure with successive Wall Street consensus estimates. The pattern is striking: analysts repeatedly projected an imminent moderation in spending, only to revise their expectations substantially higher as actual investment continued accelerating. The consensus estimate for cumulative annualized spending by the four major hyperscalers through 2028 has risen dramatically over successive forecasting periods, yet even the latest projections remain considerably below Leopold's original trajectory. The market has consistently underestimated how much physical infrastructure would be required to support successive generations of AI models, and we see little reason to believe that this forecasting bias has suddenly disappeared.

Our reasoning is straightforward. The industry is still building the foundational infrastructure required to support a technology whose ultimate economic applications remain only partially understood. Training increasingly capable models requires enormous computing resources, but inference demand could ultimately become an even larger driver of infrastructure investment as autonomous agents undertake longer tasks, coordinate with other agents, and operate continuously rather than responding to occasional user prompts. A chatbot answering a question requires a relatively modest amount of computation compared with an autonomous system conducting research, writing and testing software, evaluating alternatives, coordinating specialized agents, and repeating that process over extended periods. The economic value generated by these systems could rise substantially faster than the cost of the computation required to operate them, potentially encouraging businesses to consume far more compute even as the unit cost of intelligence declines. This is where the conventional assumption that algorithmic efficiency improvements will necessarily reduce aggregate semiconductor demand becomes questionable. Lower costs per unit of intelligence could stimulate enough additional consumption to offset efficiency gains, particularly as AI becomes capable of performing economically valuable work that was previously impossible or prohibitively expensive to automate.

This is also why we think the market's current obsession with immediate AI monetization is somewhat misplaced. Investors frequently question whether hyperscalers can generate sufficient revenue to justify hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure spending, but the appropriate framework should consider the economic value of the labor, research, and decision-making capacity that AI could eventually replace or augment. The addressable market is not limited to software subscriptions, search advertising, or existing enterprise IT expenditure. It potentially encompasses a substantial portion of global spending on intellectual labor, alongside the creation of entirely new categories of economic activity. Leopold makes an interesting distinction between the diffusion of AI across organizations and the intensification of usage within organizations that have already adopted it. His argument is that investors are paying too much attention to how many businesses have adopted AI and too little attention to how rapidly compute consumption is increasing among the most sophisticated users. The frontier laboratories themselves provide an early indication of what this future could look like, with AI usage already becoming an important component of their operating expenditure, while adoption across the broader corporate sector remains comparatively modest.

The revenue implications could be extraordinary. Leopold's team projects that OpenAI and Anthropic could collectively exit 2027 with more than $1 trillion in annualized revenue, based on the historical relationship between model capabilities and commercial adoption, adjusted for the possibility that AI development accelerates significantly. We regard this as an aggressive scenario rather than a reliable base-case forecast, particularly because converting technological capability into recognized revenue requires distribution, customer adoption, integration, and sustainable pricing. Nevertheless, the broader argument deserves serious consideration. If AI systems become capable of performing increasingly complex and valuable work, the relevant market will expand substantially beyond today's coding assistants and consumer chatbots. The more important question is therefore not whether existing AI applications are approaching saturation, but how much additional economic activity becomes addressable as the capabilities of the underlying models improve. We believe the market is still struggling to appreciate this distinction.

From an investment perspective, this reinforces our conviction in the broader AI infrastructure ecosystem, particularly leading semiconductor designers, advanced foundries, memory manufacturers, networking suppliers, and companies controlling scarce data center infrastructure. Nvidia, TSMC, and ASML remain particularly interesting because their businesses occupy strategically important positions in an industry where computational demand continues to expand and technological complexity creates formidable barriers to entry. We also see substantial opportunities across high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, optical interconnects, power distribution, cooling systems, and the physical infrastructure required to accommodate increasingly dense computing clusters. The important qualification is that structural industry growth does not automatically guarantee attractive returns for every participant, particularly in cyclical segments where capacity additions, pricing normalization, and technological substitution can eventually erode profitability. Investors must distinguish between companies benefiting from temporarily favorable supply-demand conditions and those capable of sustaining competitive advantages as the industry matures.

One particularly interesting observation in the letter concerns the extent to which market valuations have compressed despite the continued expansion of the underlying AI economy. Leopold argues that certain memory manufacturers are trading near exceptionally low multiples of his team's projected 2027 earnings, while selected data center infrastructure companies are being valued at little more than the economic value of already contracted capacity. These estimates are necessarily sensitive to assumptions about future memory prices, utilization, depreciation, and terminal values, so they should not be interpreted as definitive evidence that these companies are universally cheap. Nevertheless, they illustrate how dramatically sentiment has changed. Investors who were previously willing to extrapolate rapid growth indefinitely are now increasingly discounting a substantial slowdown, or even a prolonged deterioration, in parts of the AI infrastructure ecosystem. We believe that adjustment has created opportunities in businesses where earnings visibility remains strong, balance sheets are resilient, and valuations have already incorporated considerable pessimism.

This brings us to the recent correction in US technology and AI equities, which we continue to regard as healthy from a longer-term perspective. After an extraordinary period of appreciation, valuations and positioning had become increasingly vulnerable to changes in interest-rate expectations, concerns about AI-related financing, and uncertainty surrounding the timing of investment returns. Some degree of multiple compression was therefore inevitable, particularly in companies whose valuations assumed flawless execution. However, there is an important distinction between a correction caused by deteriorating fundamentals and one driven predominantly by a reassessment of valuation, positioning, and the cost of capital. The recent market weakness has certainly exposed vulnerabilities in more speculative and highly leveraged segments of the AI ecosystem, but we have not seen sufficient evidence to conclude that the underlying technological trajectory or long-term demand for computational infrastructure has fundamentally reversed. In fact, the sharp recovery in several leading technology and semiconductor stocks during the final week of November suggests that buying interest is beginning to return, although we would not interpret a few strong trading sessions as definitive confirmation that the correction has ended.

There is also an important lesson in Leopold's discussion of his own fund's experience during July, when Situational Awareness LP suffered a drawdown of approximately 67% despite maintaining a fundamentally bullish view on AI. I appreciate the transparency with which he acknowledges the shortcomings in portfolio construction, liquidity management, and the interaction between long and short exposures. The episode reinforces an investment principle that becomes particularly important when pursuing high-conviction structural themes: being correct about the long-term direction of an industry does not guarantee that an investor will survive the volatility required to realize that thesis. Markets can remain disconnected from fundamentals for considerably longer than anticipated, and even an ultimately correct investment thesis can produce disastrous outcomes when combined with excessive leverage, inadequate liquidity, or poor position sizing. We can agree with Leopold's assessment of AI's long-term potential while also recognizing that disciplined risk management is essential, particularly when technological disruption, regulatory uncertainty, and financial-market volatility are likely to intensify rather than diminish.

We should also acknowledge that some of the most ambitious predictions in the letter remain highly uncertain. Accelerating AI capabilities do not guarantee a smooth transition toward artificial superintelligence, and important bottlenecks remain in physical infrastructure, energy availability, data center construction, model reliability, economic adoption, and regulatory oversight. Furthermore, even if the technological progress envisioned by Leopold materializes, the distribution of economic value across publicly listed companies could change dramatically. Today's dominant technology providers may not necessarily remain the principal beneficiaries of the next generation of AI, particularly if increasingly capable systems accelerate the commoditization of intellectual property, software development, or even semiconductor design. The possibility that AI ultimately disrupts some of its current beneficiaries is an important part of the letter's argument and deserves greater attention from investors who assume that today's market leaders will maintain their competitive positions indefinitely.

Nevertheless, we believe the balance of probabilities continues to favor a prolonged expansion in AI capabilities, adoption, and the infrastructure required to support them. We do not need every projection in Leopold's letter to materialize for the investment opportunity to remain substantial. We do not necessarily need $1 trillion in AI laboratory revenue by the end of 2027, nor do we need artificial superintelligence to arrive within a particular calendar year. We simply need AI capabilities to continue improving, commercially valuable applications to expand, and the demand for computing resources to remain sufficiently strong to support continued investment across the infrastructure value chain. Given the extraordinary progress already observed, we believe these assumptions remain considerably more plausible than the increasingly pessimistic scenarios reflected in parts of the market.

Our broader conclusion is that investors may once again be making the mistake of treating the current generation of AI technology as though it represents the final stage of development. Similar skepticism accompanied earlier generations of semiconductors, cloud computing, mobile internet, and digital infrastructure, when markets repeatedly underestimated how rapidly improvements in technology could expand the range of economically viable applications. The difference today is that AI is increasingly capable of contributing to the development of its own successors, creating the possibility of technological progress occurring at a pace that conventional forecasting frameworks are poorly equipped to capture. If that dynamic continues, we could be entering a period in which the gap between technological reality and financial-market expectations becomes increasingly consequential for capital allocation.

We remain firmly bullish on AI and continue to believe that the structural investment cycle has considerably further to run. In our view, the recent correction has been a necessary and ultimately constructive adjustment after an extended period of strong performance, reducing excessive positioning and bringing valuations closer to levels that offer more attractive prospective returns. For investors establishing new positions, as well as existing shareholders looking to increase exposure to high-quality AI beneficiaries, we believe the recent weakness presents an increasingly compelling opportunity to accumulate selectively, preferably in stages and with appropriate attention to balance-sheet strength, earnings visibility, and valuation.

The central question for investors should no longer be whether AI has already experienced an extraordinary investment boom, because it unquestionably has, but whether that boom represents the culmination of the technological revolution or merely the early stages of a much larger transformation. After reading Leopold's letter and considering the accelerating evidence of AI-driven research, increasingly autonomous systems, and the enormous economic incentives to expand computational capacity, we remain convinced that we are much closer to the beginning of this transformation than its end.

Long AI. Long the infrastructure powering it.

Situational Awareness Q3 Letter: Why Memory Is "the Nvidia of the RL Era"

Leopold Aschenbrenner's fund on $SKHY, $SNDK, $MU , Kioxia & the memory trade 👇

1️⃣ The core thesis

• AI is shifting to reinforcement learning (RL) + long-running agents

• These workloads are limited by memory bandwidth, not compute power (FLOPS)

• Labs often got <5% FLOPS use from their chips; most of each chip sat idle waiting on memory

• Agents running millions of tokens need ever more KV cache, which means more memory

• Agents also need more CPU servers, adding extra DRAM demand

• Custom chips (TPUs, Trainium, ASICs) move the bidding war deeper into the supply chain, into memory

• Conclusion: memory demand grows faster than AI chip demand → a supply crunch

2️⃣ SK Hynix: the fund's largest position for most of its history

• First bought in Nov 2024 at ~₩180K, roughly a $100B company

• Pitched as "a $100B company that should be a $1T company"

• Traded at ~1x forward price/book, a historical trough, so the fund saw limited downside

• Reasons: best HBM tech (quality & yield), 30–50% discount to Micron, no new capacity possible in time

• Summer 2025: the sell-side downgraded it and fast money shorted it. The fund called it FUD and added more, partly via OTC call options

• HBM uses DRAM supply at a >3:1 ratio, which created a severe DRAM shortage

• DRAM prices 4x from 3Q25 to 3Q26; Hynix quarterly operating profit up 7x

• Hynix now earning at a pace of >$200B operating profit per year

• Peaked at ₩2.9M in summer 2026, a 16x from the fund's entry

• The fund advised Hynix against long-term agreements with price ceilings; some newer deals have price floors but no ceilings

• The fund brokered Hynix's first meeting with Anthropic and anchored Hynix's US ADR IPO as a cornerstone investor

3️⃣ NAND: Sandisk & Kioxia

• Idea: DRAM shortage → AI developers substitute NAND (historically ~40x cheaper, with 25x more bits of capacity)

• AI use case: park the KV cache in NAND instead of recomputing it on expensive GPUs/DRAM

• New products: Kioxia XL-Flash and High Bandwidth Flash (HBF), placed next to the GPU

• Supply is limited: fabs take 4 years, and makers that produce both put new capacity into DRAM

• First Sandisk buy at $11 (Sep 2025) → peak $292 (Jun 2026), >27x; now below $80

• Added heavily to Kioxia & Sandisk in Jan 2026

• NAND prices more than tripled; Kioxia & Sandisk up 4–5x from late Jan to their peaks

4️⃣ Where things stand now (Nov 2026)

• Hynix back near ₩1M, down almost two-thirds from its peak

• Hynix at ~2x 2027 earnings and ~1x end-2027 book value, on the fund's estimates; at today's price, buybacks could retire >50% of the company by end-2027

• Kioxia down ~80%, at <1x 2027 earnings (0.2x 2027+2028); could buy back ~75% of its market cap by end-2027

• The fund estimates Samsung could also buy back ~75% of its stock by end-2027

• The fund says the market is pricing a deep AI downturn starting late 2027, with memory "never making a profit again"

• Any memory pricing above that beyond 2027 = "a free call option"

• Kioxia remains one of the fund's largest positions

5️⃣ The lessons from July

• The hedge broke: the fund was short $MU against long Hynix/Kioxia

• In the crash, Micron fell ~30% while Hynix fell ~55% and Kioxia ~65%

• Puts bought as crash protection worked less well than expected

• The fund's view: watching downstream (counting chips shipped) is a lagging signal. Memory makers themselves didn't see prices going ballistic

• Its approach: start from AI technical trends, then do deep bottom-up work on companies far from SF

Wall Street had its best week in 1+ year. Nigeria's market fell. Same week. Why? 🧵

Last week, the S&P 500 sat 10%+ below its record high. Fear was loud.

This week: S&P 500 +5.6%. Nasdaq +6.7%. Dow +5.5%.

What changed? Not the world. Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia CEO on Monday. Nvidia jumped about 31.5% in one day, and the S&P 500 rose 4.7% with it.

Ask yourself: did Nvidia become 31% better in a weekend? Or did the price just move faster than the business?

Then it got messy. Tuesday and Wednesday swung hard. On Wednesday the S&P was down over 2% at one point, then clawed back to a small loss. Friday's half-day closed with a 1.6% gain at 7,297.49.

Now Lagos 🇳🇬

NGX All-Share Index: 244,912.17. Down 1.11% for the week. Down 3.69% for the month.

It did end a 7-day losing streak on Thursday, and gained 0.34% on Friday. But 55 stocks fell and only 27 rose across the week. Banks made up most of the trading volume.

Here's the part nobody tweets: the ASI is still up about 57% this year. The S&P 500 is up about 6.6%.

So who is "winning"? Ask these 3 questions before you answer:
1️⃣ Up 57% in naira. What did that return look like after inflation and the exchange rate?
2️⃣ After a big run, is a 3.7% dip a warning or a reset?
3️⃣ Did earnings change, or only prices?

Here's the lesson in plain words:
Prices move in days. Businesses move in quarters. If you can't tell the difference, headlines will run your portfolio.

FQVDM determines what you buy, while the crash framework determines when the risk/reward becomes attractive.

A US market that drops 10% and rebounds in a week is not a signal to chase. A Nigerian market that dips after a huge year is not a signal to panic. It is a signal to open your notes and re-rate your holdings.

Morning Tech Briefing — Saturday, 28 November 2026

Keywords: export controls · Black Friday rebound · $41 billion pharma deal · MCP mandate · privacy auction · NFS2ROOT

Compute now needs a licence to cross some borders. AI stocks did not wait. Neither, if a bankruptcy auction goes ahead, would millions of private chatbot conversations.

On Thursday the Financial Times reported that Nvidia had told partners to pause AI-server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries, after a new U.S. export rule took effect last week. On Friday’s short post-Thanksgiving session, the Nasdaq rose 2.31%, led by memory stocks, though Nvidia itself gained only 0.8%. The same week: Sanofi’s $41 billion purchase of Insmed, its largest deal in two decades; Google’s requirement that AI agents use official MCP servers or the Workspace CLI from 1 February 2027; a move by 42 attorneys general to stop https://t.co/YgSClWu149 auctioning more than 21 million private chats; and CVE-2026-99362, a 12-year-old Linux NFS flaw rated 9.8, with no confirmed use in the wild yet.

1. Nvidia pauses AI-server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia

On 26 November 2026, the Financial Times, citing three people familiar with the matter, reported that Nvidia had told manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers containing its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. Partners including Dell and Supermicro had told buyers in those four countries that the orders would not be allowed to ship. It was unclear whether the halt would be temporary while the companies work out how to comply. Nvidia declined to comment; Dell and Supermicro did not respond. This follows that reporting, not an official company confirmation.

The background is an interim final rule from the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security. BIS released it on 16 November; it became effective on 19 November, when published in the Federal Register. A licence is now required to export, reexport or transfer advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — five destinations BIS describes as presenting a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The reported shipment pause covers the four Southeast Asian countries, not Brazil. Separately, any data centre already providing a significant volume of computing power to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent is headquartered in, Macau or Country Group D:5, and that wishes to continue must obtain a licence within 90 days of the effective date. The aim is to close a path in which restricted entities rent advanced U.S. chips remotely through third-country data centres. The FT added that much of the region’s recent data-centre investment is in jeopardy, especially in Malaysia and Indonesia.

2. AI stocks rebound in a Black Friday half-day session — with a few figures that need care

U.S. markets were open for a shortened session on Friday, 27 November, the day after Thanksgiving, and finished higher, led by chip and other AI-linked names. Reuters put the official closes at: Nasdaq Composite up 543.70 points, or 2.31%, to 24,129.50; S&P 500 up 114.71 points, or 1.60%, to 7,297.49; Dow Jones Industrial Average up 591.99 points, or 1.18%, to 50,774.94. Some secondary write-ups rounded the Nasdaq to 24,130, the S&P 500 to 7,296, and the Dow to about 1.1%, or nearly 600 points. This briefing uses the Reuters figures.

Memory stocks led the bounce. SanDisk (SNDK) rose 15.96% to $85.36; Micron rose 7.60% to $646.95. Reuters said a broader chip gauge climbed 4.7%; Investopedia reported that the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) gained nearly 5%. Those are related but not identical, and should not be collapsed into one official Philadelphia Semiconductor Index close. Intel closed at $57.40, up 5.38%; AMD at $424.54, up 4.56%; Broadcom at $312.34, up 3.82% (often rounded to 4%); Dell at $316.96, up 6.70% (Investopedia said “nearly 7%”). Nvidia, after a weak start, ended up 0.80% at $150.49. Investopedia noted that Nvidia has lost 37% since an early-October record; Yahoo Finance shows a 6 October close of $239.24, consistent with that percentage.

The rebound followed midweek selling over AI infrastructure costs and returns. The Nasdaq should not be described as still “nearly 20%” below its October high. Yahoo Finance shows the Composite’s record close on 6 October 2026 at 27,599.79; Friday’s close of 24,129.50 is about 12.6% below that record. It had been weaker earlier: the 20 November close of 22,617.73 was about 18% below the October record — closer to, but still short of, “nearly 20%”.

Friday’s bounce also needs a half-day caveat: stock trading ended at 1:00 p.m. ET, and volume was thinner than a full session. Whether it holds will be tested on Monday. Anthropic joined the rally after briefly falling below its $83 IPO price earlier in the week. Motley Fool recorded a close of $91.88, up 10.98%; Investopedia described a 12% rise to just under $92. The close just under $92 is consistent; the exact percentage is not treated as settled.

3. Sanofi to acquire Insmed for $41 billion, its largest deal in 20 years

On Tuesday, 24 November 2026 — not Monday — Sanofi announced an agreement to acquire Insmed, a U.S. biopharmaceutical company, for $175 per share in cash, a total equity value of about $41.0 billion, or €37.6 billion. No Hong Kong-dollar conversion is given; official figures are in dollars and euros. Insmed told investors the price was a 46% premium to its unaffected close on 18 November, the day before media reports of a possible transaction. A smaller premium of about 17.5% to the last close before the announcement is a different reference point, and should not be confused with the official 46%. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to Insmed shareholder approval, U.S. and certain non-U.S. regulatory clearances, and other customary conditions.

Reuters described the purchase as Sanofi’s biggest deal in two decades. It brings two already-marketed respiratory medicines, Brinsupri (brensocatib) and Arikayce (amikacin liposome inhalation suspension), and a phase 3 candidate, treprostinil palmitil inhalation powder (TPIP). In a 27 November follow-up, Reuters reported that CEO Belen Garijo, who took office in May, said she had thought of the deal “immediately after I arrived, with a new team,” to reduce reliance on the blockbuster eczema drug Dupixent. Reuters has referred to Dupixent’s patent expiries in the early 2030s; this briefing does not treat a single 2031 date as if every relevant patent falls then. The same follow-up said Sanofi’s shares had reached a more-than-one-year high and gained 13% over the previous week.

4. Google requires AI agents to use Workspace MCP or the CLI from 1 February 2027

Also on Tuesday, 24 November, Google made eight official hosted Google Workspace MCP servers generally available — Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat and Tasks, with Keep described as coming soon — along with the official Workspace CLI, gwscli, and published a new Workspace AI Tools Addendum. Google’s developer tools reference, updated on 27 November, also lists a People API MCP server as generally available, a ninth official server not listed in the 24 November product blog.

Technical enforcement begins on 1 February 2027. From that date, AI agents or similar access tools must use Google’s Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI to access Workspace data, rather than calling Workspace REST APIs directly. Agents that keep calling the REST APIs directly are limited to Standard Tier quotas, regardless of paid tier. The Addendum’s first clause states the same requirement: a “GWS Access Tool” that is, or is driven by, an AI agent, an AI harness, or an AI model must use a Google MCP, and may not be disguised to avoid that classification.

What those servers can actually do is still settling, and should not be treated as a fixed menu. Early write-ups, including Flavio Copes on 26 November, reported that the public Gmail MCP server could search, read, manage labels and create drafts, while send, reply, forward and edit-draft tools were listed as partner-only. A 27 November independent probe found unauthenticated tools/list calls to the live Gmail endpoint flip-flopped that day: 18 of 30 requests returned 23 tools, and 12 returned 30, including send_message, reply, forward and update_draft. Google’s 27 November tools reference now documents 30 Gmail tools on the primary /mcp/v1 endpoint and 25 on /mcp/v1self; the Gmail setup guide describes sending, replying and forwarding as available, with user confirmation through form elicitation on the primary endpoint. Official pages were still being updated around launch; developers should not assume a single tools/list response is stable.

5. 42 attorneys general move to block https://t.co/YgSClWu149’s auction of more than 21 million private chats

On Tuesday, 24 November, California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced that a bipartisan coalition of 42 attorneys general — 41 states and the District of Columbia, not 42 states — had objected in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware to https://t.co/YgSClWu149’s plan to auction its platform and the private chat histories of more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including more than 2.1 million registered to minors, plus personal data such as IP addresses. (The same California release once quotes Bonta as saying “45 attorneys general”; the formal count in the release and the state list is 42, used here.) The auction is set for 1 December 2026; a sale hearing is set for 3 and 4 December.

The only disclosed bidder so far, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, was formed in Delaware on 13 November and selected the next day as the stalking-horse bidder. Court notices describe the bid as $10 million in cash plus assumed liabilities, with a $350,000 termination or break-up fee. The attorneys general argue that https://t.co/YgSClWu149 had told users it would not sell personal information — the California release quotes its privacy policy: “we do not sell personal information for monetary consideration” — yet the proposed terms impose no meaningful constraints on the buyer, who could resell the data without disclosure and would not have to honour the existing privacy policy or users’ deletion requests. Disney has a separate $20 million non-exclusive licence for https://t.co/YgSClWu149 technology that, per reporting and court notices, does not include user chats; that transaction has not received final court approval, and a similar coalition has already objected to it.

6. NFS2ROOT: a 12-year-old Linux NFS flaw, CVE-2026-99362, rated 9.8

A critical vulnerability in the Linux kernel’s NFS server was assigned CVE-2026-99362 on 19 November 2026 and has been called NFS2ROOT. The European Union Vulnerability Database lists a CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.8 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H). Public reporting describes a heap buffer overflow in the in-kernel NFS server (nfsd) when handling NFSv4.1 or NFSv4.2 sessions. The weakness has been present since Linux 3.16, released in March 2014 — about 12 years.

At a high level, an unauthenticated attacker who can reach a vulnerable server may be able to obtain root privileges, with no user interaction required. This briefing does not describe how. OpenSec has published a video demonstration of a remote root shell and said the exploit remains private. As of BleepingComputer’s 27 November report, there were no reports of exploitation in the wild. The flaw was found independently by Jérémy Jean of France’s ANSSI, who submitted a fix in August, and by OpenSec, which reported it to maintainers in September. Patched versions listed by CSO, and in the EU vulnerability record, include 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193, 6.6.163, 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1.

Daily quotation

“If a person takes no thought for what is distant, there will be worries close at hand.”
— Confucius, Analects, Wei Ling Gong. Many editions number this as chapter 12 (15.12); some Chinese chapterizations number it 15.11. The line is 人无远虑，必有近忧.

The two main threads of the week fit the warning. Export controls are plugging an immediate hole in the compute map; the longer effects on a fast-growing regional buildout are still being counted. Markets chased a half-day bounce, with a full Monday session still to come. Those who lack a long view are rarely short of nearby worries.

Explainer: What is MCP, and why is Google tightening this channel?

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard announced by Anthropic on 25 November 2024 to unify how AI models connect to external tools and data. Before MCP, each model typically needed a custom connector for each tool — N models times M tools. MCP standardises that interface.

The protocol groups a server’s capabilities into three primitives: Resources (readable data), Prompts (reusable templates) and Tools (actions the model can invoke). Routing Workspace access through Google’s official MCP servers means the operator of the server also decides what an agent may do. High-risk actions can be gated or made to require confirmation; quotas and billing sit with Google.

Researchers have already warned that this convenience brings a new attack surface: a tool’s text description can be seeded with hidden instructions (tool poisoning), leading a model to take unauthorised actions; content retrieved through a tool can also carry indirect prompt injection. Google’s mandate pulls this channel back under the platform’s hand.

Anchor papers: Hou, X. et al. (2025). “Model Context Protocol (MCP): Landscape, Security Threats, and Future Research Directions.” arXiv:2503.23278. Gaire, S. et al. (2025). “Systematization of Knowledge: Security and Safety in the Model Context Protocol Ecosystem.” arXiv:2512.08290.

Nvidia asked four countries to wait for a licence. AI stocks did not wait until Monday. If the https://t.co/YgSClWu149 auction goes ahead, the secrets people told a chatbot would not have to wait at all.

——

晨间科技早报 — 2026年11月28日（星期六）

今日关键词：出口管制 · 黑色星期五反弹 · 410亿美元药业并购 · MCP强制令 · 隐私拍卖 · NFS2ROOT

算力过关，现在要批文。AI股没有等。若破产拍卖成立，上千万段与聊天机器人的私密对话，同样不必等。

星期四，《金融时报》报道，在美国新的出口管制上周生效后，Nvidia已通知合作伙伴，暂停向东南亚四国付运AI服务器。星期五的感恩节后半日市，纳斯达克综合指数上涨2.31%，存储芯片股领涨，Nvidia本身只升0.8%。同一星期还有：Sanofi以410亿美元收购Insmed，为20年来最大交易；Google要求AI代理自2027年2月1日起经官方MCP服务器或Workspace命令行工具访问Workspace数据；42位检察长要求阻止https://t.co/YgSClWu149拍卖逾2100万段私人对话；以及潜伏约12年的Linux NFS漏洞CVE-2026-99362，评分9.8，目前尚无已确认的野外利用。

1. Nvidia暂停向马来西亚、新加坡、泰国及印尼付运AI服务器

2026年11月26日，《金融时报》引述三名知情人士报道，Nvidia已通知制造合作伙伴，停止向马来西亚、新加坡、泰国和印尼付运载有其芯片的服务器。Dell与Supermicro等合作伙伴已告知四国买家，相关订单将不准出货。暂停是暂时的，还是在各方摸清如何符合新规之前的安排，报道称仍不清楚。Nvidia拒绝置评；Dell与Supermicro未回应。本条按报道口径表述，并非官方确认。

背景是美国商务部工业与安全局（BIS）的临时最终规则。BIS于11月16日发布，11月19日在《联邦公报》公布并生效。向印度尼西亚、马来西亚、新加坡、泰国或巴西出口、再出口或境内转移先进半导体，现须申领许可证——BIS称这五个目的地存在高于通常水平的转移风险。报道中的停运范围是东南亚四国，不包括巴西。另外，在规则公布前，已向总部或其最终母公司位于澳门或D:5国家组的企业提供大量算力、并希望继续的数据中心，须在生效日起90日内取得许可证。规则旨在堵截受限实体经第三国数据中心远程租用美国先进芯片的途径。《金融时报》称，新限制已使该地区近期数据中心投资面临风险，马来西亚和印尼尤甚。

2. AI股在黑色星期五半日市反弹——若干数字须慎读

美国股市于11月27日（星期五，感恩节后的半日市）收高，芯片及其他AI相关股票领涨。路透社给出的收盘价为：纳斯达克综合指数升543.70点，或2.31%，收报24,129.50点；标普500指数升114.71点，或1.60%，收报7,297.49点；道琼斯工业平均指数升591.99点，或1.18%，收报50,774.94点。部分二次报道将纳指写作24,130点、标普写作7,296点，道指升幅写作约1.1%、近600点。本篇采用路透社数字。

存储芯片股升幅居前。SanDisk（SNDK）升15.96%，收报85.36美元；美光升7.60%，收报646.95美元。路透社称更广的芯片指标升4.7%；Investopedia则报道iShares半导体ETF（SOXX）升近5%。两者相关但并不等同，不宜写成费城半导体指数的单一官方收盘。英特尔收报57.40美元，升5.38%；AMD收报424.54美元，升4.56%；博通收报312.34美元，升3.82%（常被约作4%）；戴尔收报316.96美元，升6.70%（Investopedia写作「近7%」）。Nvidia开局偏弱，收报150.49美元，升0.80%。Investopedia指出，该股自10月初纪录高位以来已跌37%；雅虎财经显示10月6日收于239.24美元，与这一比例相符。

此轮反弹出现在周中因AI基建成本与回报承压的抛售之后。不宜写成纳指仍较10月高位「跌近两成」。雅虎财经显示，纳斯达克综合指数于2026年10月6日创下27,599.79点的纪录收盘价；周五收盘24,129.50点，较大约低12.6%。本月早些时候跌得更深：11月20日收于22,617.73点，较10月纪录收盘价约低18%，更接近、但仍未达到「近两成」。

周五的反弹还需加上半日市的提醒：股票交易于美东时间下午1时结束，成交较全日偏少。反弹能否延续，仍待星期一全日交易检验。Anthropic亦加入反弹，该股本周早些时候曾短暂跌破83美元的招股价。Motley Fool记录收盘价为91.88美元，升10.98%；Investopedia将升幅描述为12%，收于略低于92美元。收于略低于92美元是一致的；精确升幅在此不作为已核实的单一数字。

3. Sanofi以410亿美元收购Insmed，为20年来最大交易

2026年11月24日（星期二，不是星期一），Sanofi宣布协议收购美国生物制药公司Insmed，价格为每股175美元现金，股权价值约410亿美元，或376亿欧元。（不换算港元，官方数字为美元与欧元。）Insmed向投资者说明，该价格较11月18日——媒体报道可能交易的前一日——未受影响的收盘价溢价46%。另有约17.5%的溢价是相对于宣布前最后收盘价，参考时点不同，不应与官方的46%混为一谈。交易预计于2027年上半年完成，须待Insmed股东批准、美国及部分其他司法管辖区的监管批准，以及其他惯常条件。

路透社称，这是Sanofi 20年来最大的收购。买入的是两款已上市呼吸道药物Brinsupri（brensocatib）与Arikayce（amikacin liposome inhalation suspension），以及临床三期候选药物treprostinil palmitil inhalation powder（TPIP）。在11月27日跟进报道中，路透社引述5月上任的行政总裁Belen Garijo说，她「一到任，和新团队一起」就想到了这笔交易，目的之一是降低对王牌湿疹药Dupixent的依赖。路透社将Dupixent的专利到期表述为2030年代初；本篇不以某一个2031年日期，当作所有相关专利均在当年到期。同一篇报道称，Sanofi股价升至逾一年高位，过去一周上涨13%。

4. Google强制AI代理改行MCP或CLI通道，2027年2月1日起执行

同样在11月24日（星期二），Google将八个官方托管的Google Workspace MCP服务器正式推出——Gmail、Drive、Docs、Sheets、Slides、Calendar、Chat和Tasks，并称Keep即将推出——同时推出官方命令行工具gwscli，并发布新的《Workspace AI Tools Addendum》。Google于11月27日更新的开发者工具说明，亦将People API MCP服务器列为已正式推出，即第9个官方服务器，不在24日产品博客所列八个之中。

技术强制自2027年2月1日起执行。自该日起，AI代理或类似访问工具访问Workspace数据时，必须使用Google的Workspace MCP服务器或Workspace CLI，不得直接调用Workspace REST API。继续直连REST API的代理，不论所选用的付费等级，一律被限制在Standard级配额。增编首条规定了同一要求：由AI代理、AI框架（AI Harness）或AI模型驱动的「GWS Access Tool」必须使用Google MCP，不得伪装以规避这一分类。

这些服务器究竟能做些什么，目前仍未完全定型，不宜当成固定菜单。早期文章（包括Flavio Copes 11月26日的实测）称，公开版Gmail MCP服务器可以搜索、阅读、管理标签和创建草稿，而发送、回复、转发和修改草稿被列为合作伙伴专用。11月27日的一项独立探测发现，对Gmail线上tools/list接口的未认证请求在同一天来回切换：30次中18次返回23项工具，12次返回30项，较长清单包含send_message、reply、forward和update_draft。Google于11月27日更新的工具参考，已把主端点/mcp/v1的Gmail工具数记为30项，回退端点/mcp/v1self为25项；Gmail配置指南也将发送、回复和转发列为可用能力，并在主端点上通过表格征求用户确认。上线前后官方页面仍在更新，开发者不应假设单次tools/list结果不变。

5. 42位检察长联手阻止https://t.co/YgSClWu149拍卖逾2100万段私人对话

11月24日（星期二），加州检察长Rob Bonta宣布，一个由42位检察长组成的跨党派联盟——是41个州加上哥伦比亚特区，不是42个州——已向美国特拉华州破产法院提出反对，要求阻止破产中的https://t.co/YgSClWu149拍卖其平台，以及逾2100万个美国账户的私人对话记录，其中逾210万个账户登记为未成年人，并包括IP地址等个人资料。（同一份加州新闻稿在引用Bonta讲话时，有一处写作「45位检察长」；正文和州名单中的正式数字是42，本篇采用42。）拍卖定于2026年12月1日举行；出售聆讯定于12月3日至4日。

目前唯一已披露的竞投者Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC于11月13日在特拉华州成立，次日即被选为底价竞投者（stalking horse）。法庭通知将出价记为1000万美元现金，另加承担若干负债，并设35万美元终止费或分手费。检察长一方指出，https://t.co/YgSClWu149曾向用户表示不会出售个人信息——加州新闻稿引用其隐私政策：「我们不会为金钱对价出售个人信息」——但拟议条款对买家几乎没有约束，买家可转售数据而不作披露，也不必遵守现有隐私政策或处理用户的删除请求。迪士尼另以2000万美元取得https://t.co/YgSClWu149技术的非独家授权，报道和法庭通知称该交易不包括用户对话；尚未获法院最终批准，类似联盟此前已提出反对。

6. NFS2ROOT：Linux内核潜伏12年的NFS漏洞，CVE-2026-99362，评分9.8

Linux内核NFS服务器中的一个严重漏洞于2026年11月19日获编配CVE-2026-99362，称作NFS2ROOT。欧盟漏洞数据库给出的CVSS v3.1基础评分为9.8（AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H）。公开报道称，这是内核NFS服务器（nfsd）在处理NFSv4.1或NFSv4.2会话时的堆缓冲区溢出，自Linux 3.16（2014年3月发布）起即存在，已约12年。

就公开的高层事实而言，未经认证的攻击者若能接触到存在漏洞的服务器，即可能取得root权限，且无需用户交互。本篇不描述利用方式。OpenSec已发布远程取得root shell的演示视频，并称利用代码仍不公开。截至BleepingComputer 11月27日的报道，未见野外利用报告。该漏洞由法国国家信息系统安全局（ANSSI）研究员Jérémy Jean与OpenSec各自独立发现；Jean于8月提交修补，OpenSec于9月向维护者报告。CSO列举、并与欧盟漏洞记录相符的修补版本包括：5.10.275、5.15.226、6.1.193、6.6.163、6.12.117、6.18.61、7.3.2及7.4-rc1。

新知识科普：MCP是什么？为何Google要收紧这条通道？

MCP（Model Context Protocol，模型上下文协议）是Anthropic于2024年11月25日公布的开放标准，用以统一AI模型接驳外部工具与数据的方式。在此之前，每个模型要接每个工具，往往都要各自编写接驳器——N个模型乘M个工具。MCP把这套接口标准化。

协议把服务器能力分成三种原语：Resources（只读数据）、Prompts（可复用提示模板）和Tools（可执行的操作）。把Workspace接驳点收归Google官方MCP服务器，意味着谁控制服务器，谁就决定代理能做什么：高风险操作可以被关上或改为需要确认，配额与计费也由Google掌握。

学术界已经提醒，这种便利伴随着新的攻击面：工具的文字描述可被植入隐藏指令（工具投毒），使模型执行未授权操作；经工具取回的外部内容，也可能夹带间接提示注入。Google的强制令，正是把这条通道收回到平台之手。

锚点文献：Hou et al. (2025), arXiv:2503.23278；Gaire et al. (2025), arXiv:2512.08290。全文题名见上文。

2126544522691719216.text:
Nasdaq ripped 6.68% this week. Bitcoin managed about 2%.

Everyone calls that decoupling. I think bitcoin has never been chained to Wall Street this tightly.

Quick numbers. The Nasdaq 100 lost more than 10% the week before, its worst week since 2020. Three and a half sessions later the S&P was up 5.6%, best week since April 2025. Bitcoin? Seven straight red weeks, a two-year low around $57,244 on Wednesday, chopping near $60K into Friday's close, still down about 20% for November.

Follow the money. Per FinScans, spot bitcoin ETFs bled $1.79B the prior week, $1.37B of it from $IBIT alone. Another ~$570M left Monday, ~$453M Wednesday. November is now the worst month of outflows these ETFs have ever had.

The lazy read: crypto winter, retail lost faith.

My read: the buyer changed.

A few years ago the marginal bid was retail with USDT and miners. Today it's a PM sitting behind an ETF with a risk budget, and bitcoin lives in the same bucket as Nvidia. CME has a December 9 hike priced at 98%+. The 10 year sits near 4.9%, real yields above 2%. You have to cut gross. One asset reports earnings every quarter. The other produces zero cash flow. Which one goes first?

The flows already answered.

Darker detail: on Thanksgiving, stocks were closed and bitcoin was open 24/7. If you needed liquidity over the holiday, there was exactly one ATM in the building. The ETF made BTC the easiest thing in the portfolio to sell. In a bull market that's called liquidity. In this tape it's called supply.

We've seen this movie. 2013: Bernanke starts talking taper, real yields climb, the S&P rallies almost 30%, gold drops 28%, and GLD sheds roughly 40% of its bullion in a year. Gold ETFs were also sold as the front door for institutions. The door worked fine. Both directions.

One more number. AMBCrypto estimated earlier this year that the average spot ETF buyer sits around $82K. That's 35%+ above here. Every rally runs into a wall of people who just want to get back to even, and a breakeven seller is more stubborn than ten shorts.

My call: as long as the Nasdaq doesn't crack again, BTC still can't reclaim $70K before year end, and spot ETFs post net outflows for December too. If bitcoin closes the year above $70K and December flows flip net positive, I'm wrong and the allocators came back.

They called it digital gold for a decade. This year it finally earned the name. 2013 gold, specifically.

From January to October 2026, the sales profit margin of China's auto industry stood at just 3.2%, dipping further to 1.9% in October alone. Data disclosed by Cui Dongshu, Secretary-General of the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), shows that over the first 10 months, industry-wide revenue reached RMB 9.0589 trillion (+1.9% YoY), costs hit RMB 8.0809 trillion (+3.2% YoY), and total profit plunged 26% YoY to RMB 286.7 billion. In October alone, monthly profit came in at RMB 19.1 billion, with the YoY decline widening to 53%.

Behind the steadily declining margins lies two-way pressure across both the upstream and downstream ends of the industrial chain. Against the backdrop of local governments advancing the "Two New" policies (large-scale equipment upgrades and consumer goods trade-ins) to unleash domestic demand, earnings improvement in the auto sector has lagged noticeably behind other consumer goods. Meanwhile, rising oil prices alongside surging profits in upstream non-ferrous metals and semiconductors have pushed up vehicle manufacturing costs, while wait-and-see sentiment among end buyers has constrained automakers' room to pass those costs through on pricing.

Remarks from executives at leading automakers also corroborate these cost pressures. Richard Yu (Yu Chengdong) recently revealed at the Stelato V8 launch event that due to high safety protection standards and solid materials, the cost of a single 120 kWh battery pack has approached the RMB 100,000 range, resulting in situations where they "can't outcompete rivals and sometimes even take a loss."

What remains to be observed and verified is when automakers will reach an inflection point for profitability recovery as "anti-involution" efforts continue, while the divergence in per-vehicle gross margins across manufacturers and specific battery pack BOM cost breakdowns also await further disclosure in upcoming earnings reports and official statements.

2026年1—10月，中国汽车行业销售利润率仅为3.2%，10月单月进一步下探至1.9%。乘联分会秘书长崔东树披露的数据显示，前10个月全行业收入90589亿元（同比增1.9%），成本80809亿元（同比增3.2%），利润总额2867亿元，同比大降26%；10月单月利润191亿元，同比降幅扩大至53%。

利润率持续走低的背后，是产业链上下游的双向承压。在各地推进“两新”政策释放内需的背景下，汽车行业效益改善幅度明显落后于其他消费品；与此同时，油价上涨以及上游有色金属、半导体利润暴增推高了整车制造成本，终端购车观望情绪又限制了车企在价格端的传导空间。

一线车企的高管表态也侧面印证了成本压力。余承东近日在享界V8发布会上透露，由于对安全防护定出高标准且用料扎实，一块120度电池包的成本已逼近十万元价格段位，甚至出现“干不过别人、有时候还亏损”的情况。

目前仍待观察和证实的是：随着反内卷工作持续推进，整车厂何时能够迎来盈利修复拐点，各家车企单车毛利分化与具体电池包BOM成本明细也有待后续财报和官方口径进一步披露。

Friday was a half-day session after Thanksgiving — stocks closed at 1 PM ET. The indices didn’t treat it like a holiday. S&P 500 up 1.6% to 7297.49; Nasdaq up 2.3% to 24129.50; Dow up 1.2% to 50774.94; Russell 2000 up 1.7%. Growth clearly led: the tech sector ETF gained 2.8%, discretionary and communication services followed, while healthcare, utilities, and staples barely moved. Large and small caps were roughly in line, with the Russell a bit faster. All 11 sector ETFs finished green, but this was a thin half-day — take the gains with a grain of salt.

The hottest names were almost all in tech and semiconductors. $SNDK ripped 15.96%, the strongest in storage; $MU rose 7.60% on heavy volume; $ANT jumped 10.98% and reclaimed its $83 IPO price; $TSLA gained 5.22% and closed exactly at $400; $AMD up 4.56%; $AMZN up 3.96%, the biggest single contributor to the S&P; $META up 3.13%. The most actively traded name, $NVDA, only managed +0.80% to close at $150.49 — it gave back the premarket pop of roughly 4% and still finished green.

What got reinforced today is that the market is buying the tech and semiconductor names that got hit on Wednesday, especially storage. Before the open some people said the move was just futures short-covering on a thin holiday tape. Once the cash market opened, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 4.7% — money actually went into the stocks. The half-day caveat still applies; Monday needs another look.

Three things to watch before Monday’s open. Futures from Sunday night into Monday morning — whether Friday’s storage and semi gains can hold. China’s official manufacturing PMI comes out Monday morning Beijing time, before the US open. On rates, the 10-year closed Friday at 4.94% and was rising that day; another 25 bp in December is almost fully priced. After the open there’s Chicago PMI; the bigger one this week is Friday’s jobs report.

Storage put up double-digit moves today while Nvidia couldn’t hold its premarket pop. Filling the dip, or is the leader already starting to loosen? Not investment advice.

📉 Bitcoin bear markets: is the bottom getting close?

Past Bitcoin bear markets, measured from cycle peak to bottom, have followed a similar timeline:

🔹 2013 to 2015: about 13 to 14 months 🔹 2017 to 2018: about 12 months 🔹 2021 to 2022: about 12 to 13 months

In each past cycle, the bottom came roughly a year to 14 months after the peak. Bitcoin's current cycle is now in its 14th month since the October 2025 high, which puts it right in that historical window.

That doesn't mean the bottom is in. Bitcoin fell below $58,000 on 21 November, its lowest since July, so it's still making new lows. The timeline says watch closely, but the price hasn't confirmed anything yet.

The signs that would matter are a higher low, a return of steady ETF inflows and Bitcoin reclaiming key levels and holding them.

History doesn't guarantee what happens next, and timing alone has never called a bottom.

【Bitcoin分析】
BTC 4年周期の次の"底"はどこや？

先週の4年周期の投稿、めちゃくちゃ見てもらえたから続き出すで。
今回はみんな一番気になっとる「次の底、いつ・どこ・どう動くか」や。

先に言うとく。
底で一番損するのは「怖くなって全部投げた奴」や。
これ読んで同じミスだけはせんといてな？

■ 過去の暴落、ガチの数字

2017年12月 天井 約20,089ドル
→ 2018年12月 底 約3,191ドル
＝ -84%（約12ヶ月）

2021年11月 天井 約68,790ドル
→ 2022年11月 底 約15,599ドル
＝ -77%（約12ヶ月）

天井から"約1年"かけて、8割前後吹っ飛んどる。
しかも下落率は -84% → -77% と、回を追うごとにちょっとずつマイルドになっとるんよ。

■ で、今回はどうや

2025年10月 史上最高値 約126,198ドル
今（11/21時点）約57,500ドル前後
＝ 天井からもう -54%

天井から約13ヶ月。
過去のパターンやと「そろそろ底を探しにいく時期」に入っとる。
前回の動画の見立てやと、本命の底は2027年あたり。
つまり今〜2027年は"底ゾーン"の可能性があるってことや。

■ もし今回も同じなら？

126,198ドルから
・-70%なら → 約38,000ドル
・-77%なら → 約29,000ドル
・-84%なら → 約20,000ドル

これは「過去と同じ動きをしたら」っていう計算なだけで予想ちゃうで。
ETFや機関マネーが入っとる今回は、もっと浅い底で終わるパターンも全然ありえる。

■ 両シナリオ

🟢 強気 : 今の5万ドル台あたりで下げ止まって、早めに底打ち
🔴 弱気：過去通り-70%以上掘って、3万ドル台まで一段下げ

どっちに転んでも慌てへん準備だけしとけ。

■ 初心者が底で生き残るルール

①全力で買うな
「ここが底や！」って一発で全ツッパする奴が一番焼かれる。
底は後からしか分からん。

②分割で拾え（ドルコスト平均法）
毎月◯万円とか、◯%下がるごとに少しずつ。
これなら下がっても「安く買えるやん」って思える。

③パニック売りすな
過去の底は、みんなが「ビットコイン終わった」って言うてた時や。
一番怖い時に投げた奴が一番損しとる。

④高レバは触るな
底ゾーンは上下にめちゃくちゃ振られる。
レバかけとったら、方向合ってても途中で狩られて退場や。

⑤生活費・借金で買うな
余剰資金だけ。これが握力の源や。

天井で浮かれた奴が損して、
底で黙って拾った奴が次の天井で笑う。
これを毎回繰り返しとるのがビットコインや。

最後にこの動画見といてな↓

💯 @Bitcoin: the holiday bounce didn't last long. 

On Thursday, US stock markets took the day off for Thanksgiving, while crypto continued trading as usual. This created an interesting situation: Bitcoin traded around the clock, but US spot ETFs, through which many investors gain exposure to crypto, were temporarily closed.

Against this backdrop, BTC bounced from $57,500 and climbed back above $61,000. Ethereum and major altcoins followed. However, the rebound looked more like a technical bounce than a genuine shift in market sentiment. On the morning of November 27, Bitcoin short liquidations amounted to around $65M, compared with $20M in long liquidations. In other words, part of the rally was driven by short covering rather than a massive influx of new buyers.

The ETF flows were also telling. Before the holiday, US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $453M in outflows in a single day. From November 2 through November 25, cumulative net outflows had reached $5.39B. There were no new figures on Thursday because the markets were closed, while Friday's trading session in the US was shortened.

There's also an interesting development in traditional finance.

The European Council nominated Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next ECB president. He is known for supporting the tokenization of bank deposits. This means bringing traditional bank money onto the blockchain without changing its underlying nature — it remains a liability of a commercial bank.

💎 For the crypto industry, this is a mixed signal. On the one hand, blockchain is becoming increasingly integrated into the traditional financial system. On the other, tokenized deposits could compete with stablecoins in payments and settlements.

On Friday, after US markets reopened, Bitcoin dropped to $58,729, falling back below the psychological $59,000 level. The crypto market got nothing more than a brief respite from the prolonged sell-off. For now, sellers remain in control.
